text: By the time the first winter rains reached the low stone arches of Thessaly Weir last week, the answer to a question long asked by schoolchildren and canal engineers alike was once again plain: the structure diverts the Morrow. Built in 1898 to tame flood surges on the eastern flats, the weir has since become a quiet hinge in Northfold’s water system, sending a measured share of the river into the Southmere Channel before the remainder bends onward toward Alder Reach. Water authority records show the diversion has averaged 42 million gallons a day this season, slightly above last year’s figure. Residents of Old Kestrel still speak of the Morrow’s “split voice,” a reminder that even a river can be made to serve two futures.
